---
title: "Smooth Morphisms"
subtitle: ""
---

A smooth morphism is the relative version of a nonsingular variety. Roughly, its fibers are smooth and fit together uniformly over the base.

::: {.callout-tip title="Mental picture"}
Think of a smooth morphism as a family of manifolds whose dimension stays constant and whose members do not suddenly acquire singularities.
:::

## Defitions
:::{#def-standard-smooth-morphism name="standard smooth morphism"}

The projection

$$
\operatorname{Spec}(R[x_1,\cdot, \cdot, x_{n+r}]/(f_1,\cdot, f_r)) \longrightarrow \operatorname{Spec}(R)
$$

is called the standard smooth morphism of relative dimension $n$ if the determinant of the matrix 

$$
\left(\frac{\partial f_i}{\partial x_j}\right)_{1\leq i,j\leq r}
$$

is invertible in the ring $R[x_1,\cdot, \cdot, x_{n+r}]/(f_1,\cdot, f_r)$. 
:::

:::{#rem-jacobson name=""}
The fibers of this morphism are smooth varieties of dimension $n$ by the Jacobian criterion. The condition on the determinant is a relative version of the Jacobian criterion.
:::

:::{#def-smooth-morphism name="smooth morphism"}
A morphism $f\colon X\to Y$ between schemes is **smooth** of relative dimension $n$ if there exist open coverings $\{U_i\}$ of $X$ and $\{V_i\}$ of $Y$ such that $f(U_i)\subseteq V_i$ and for each $i$, the restriction $f|_{U_i}\colon U_i\to V_i$ is a standard smooth morphism of relative dimension $n$.
:::

:::{#def-smooth-variety name="smooth variety"}
A variety $X$ over a field $k$ is **smooth** if the structure morphism $X\to \operatorname{Spec}(k)$ is smooth. 
:::

:::{.callout-tip title=""}
Such definition for smooth variety is a little bit indirect, but it is convenient for our discussion since we will not spend much time on smooth varieties.
:::

## Basic properties
:::{#prp-smooth-morphism-composition name=""}
If $f\colon X\to Y$ and $g\colon Y\to Z$ are smooth morphisms of relative dimension $n$ and $m$ respectively, then the composition $g\circ f\colon X\to Z$ is also smooth of relative dimension $n+m$.
:::
:::{.proof}
This is a local property, so we can assume that $f$ and $g$ are standard smooth morphisms of relative dimension $n$ and $m$ respectively. Then, by the chain rule, the corresponding Jacobian matrix of the composition $g\circ f$ is a block-upper-triangular matrix with the Jacobian matrices of $f$ and $g$ on the diagonal. Therefore, the determinant of the corresponding square matrix of $g\circ f$ is the product of determinants of the square matrices of $f$ and $g$, which are both invertible. So $g\circ f$ is a standard smooth morphism of relative dimension $n+m$.
:::

### Relation to differentials
We recall the definition and properties of the sheaf of differentials in [Unramified Morphisms](unramified-morphisms.qmd). The sheaf of differentials can be used to characterize smooth morphisms and smooth varieties.

:::{#prp-differentials-of-smooth-varieties name=""}
A variety $X$ over $k$ is smooth if and only if the sheaf of differentials $\Omega_{X/k}$ is locally free of rank $\dim(X)$.
:::

:::{.proof}
When $\Omega_{X/k}$ is locally free of rank $\dim(X)$, we know that the Jacobian matrix has full rank at every point, which implies that $X$ is smooth. Conversely, assume $X$ is smooth. Then, by the relation between smoothness and regualrness, one can show that $X$ is reduced. Since $X$ is of finite type, the sheaf of differentials $\Omega_{X/k}$ is of finite type. By the relation between the cotangent space and the fibre of the sheaf of differentials, we have $\dim_{k(x)}(\Omega_{X/k}\otimes k(x))=\dim(X)$ for all closed points $x\in X$. Therefore, we conclude that $\Omega_{X/k}$ is locally free of rank $\dim(X)$.
:::

:::{.callout-caution title="Caution"}
It is not easy to show that a smooth variety is reduced. The proof is not included here, but it can be found in the textbook "The Rising Sea". And the last statement in the proof above is a corollary of Nakayama's lemma, which is a fundamental result in alegbraic geometry, and both reducedness, finiteness and the constantness of the dimension of fibre matter. See 14.3.J in "The Rising Sea" for details.
:::

:::{#prp-smooth-and transitive-exact-sequence name=""}
Let $f\colon X\to Y$ and $g\colon Y\to Z$ be morphisms of schemes. If $f$ and $g$ are smooth, then the transitive exact sequence is exact on the left, too, which means that the sequence
$$
0\to f^*\Omega_{Y/Z}\to \Omega_{X/Z}\to \Omega_{X/Y}\to 0
$$

is exact.
:::

:::{.proof}
This is a local property, so we can assume that $f$ and $g$ are standard smooth morphisms of relative dimension $n$ and $m$ respectively. Then, by @lem-derivation-of-polynomial-ring, we know the module of differentials is the cokernel of the Jacobian matrix. The injectivity of the left follows from the fact that the Jacobian matrix of $g\circ f$ is a block-upper-triangular matrix with the Jacobian matrices of $f$ and $g$ on the diagonal.
:::
